newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin out of clinic, but faces new headaches.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin out of clinic, but faces new headaches.

text.p: Exactly a month after surgeons gave him a new lease on life with a heart bypass operation, President Boris Yeltsin will spend his first full day outside a clinic on Thursday. But his political headaches may just be starting.

The normally compliant upper chamber of parliament, the Federation Council, was in uncharacteristic uproar on Wednesday after Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, pleading illness, refused to appear to explain how he planned to solve an economic crisis whose latest manifestation is a national coal strike.
Some Council members, who are drawn from Russia's regional leaders, called for a motion of no confidence in Chernomyrdin's government and questioned its ability to handle the situation.

The 89 regional governors who make up half the upper chamber used to be nominated by Yeltsin. But elections this autumn have replaced some governors with his opponents and given others the independence that comes with a popular mandate.

The liberal governor of Nizhny Novgorod region, Boris Nemtsov, told Council speaker Yegor Stroyev during the debate: "You've got to go to Chernomyrdin and ask him if he has the will and the courage to work on in this post or not."

"If we don't take steps, then...the people will rise up and millions will take to the streets," warned Vladimir Shtygashev, parliamentary speaker of the Khakasia region in Siberia, where thousands of miners are on strike over months of unpaid wages.

The government took the unusual step of issuing a statement, stressing its "readiness for constructive and permanent dialogue with the federal legislature in solving our toughest social problems" but expressing "astonishment" at deputies' exploitation of "cheap popularity and irresponsible speculation".

The State Duma lower house, which is dominated by Yeltsin's communist opponents, has already been giving the government a hard time. It rejected its 1997 budget and lambasted a decision to pull troops out of Chechnya after nearly two years of war and effectively to recognise the region's separatist leadership.
Yeltsin, 65, is due to meet Council speaker Stroyev on Thursday at a residence in the village of Gorky-9 near Moscow, where he moved on Wednesday from the nearby Barvikha sanatorium.
"Thank you for your truly selfless work," a smiling Yeltsin told a group of doctors as he left the third medical facility he had been in since his operation on November 5.
Medical staff expect him back in the Kremlin this month.
One doctor assured Yeltsin: "Everything will be all right."
He was presumably talking about the president's health. The state of Russia's economy and the government's finances scarcely gives grounds for optimism about the immediate future.
Chernomyrdin will chair a cabinet meeting on Thursday dominated by economic problems, including the coal strike.
Miners' leaders, who helped Yeltsin to electoral success in 1991, said on Wednesday they would continue until the government paid out previously promised subsidies.
First Deputy Prime Minister Vladimir Potanin was despatched to the key Kuzbass region in Siberia to talk to the miners.

The government says it is strapped by huge tax arrears, especially from big companies. A massive shortfall in tax revenue prompted the International Monetary Fund to hold up loan payments and prompted the Duma to reject the 1997 budget.

The latest victims of the growing web of unpaid bills were the Dynamo Moscow basketball team. Owed wages since July, they threatened to strike. But the sports-loving Yeltsin stepped in with a decree ordering the government to help the club out.
The rest of the nation's problems may be harder to fix.
